name: Protectionism
summary: Protectionism is the doctrine and policy of shielding a country's own producers from foreign competition through tariffs, import quotas, bounties and other government aid. Its modern theorists, from Hamilton's Report on Manufactures through List, Carey and Patten, argue that a nation needs a developed manufacturing industry for its wealth, independence and security, that free trade between unequally developed nations keeps the weaker dependent, and that government should actively foster new industries, at first temporarily (the infant-industry argument) and in later versions permanently.
scope: Modern protectionism as the reference works define it: a policy of trade barriers protecting domestic import-competing industry (Bhagwati; the Encyclopedia.com entries) and the body of doctrine that the 1911 Britannica traces from Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (1791) through Friedrich List's National System of Political Economy, Henry C. Carey and Simon Patten. Earlier mercantilism (bullion and the balance of trade) has its own profile and is left out, as are the platforms of particular protectionist parties (the US Republican tariff party, British tariff reform), which the sources describe as history, not as the doctrine's tenets. Where its theorists disagree the answer is a split.

furtherReading.title: Protectionism (Concise Encyclopedia of Economics)
furtherReading.note: A short account by trade economist Jagdish Bhagwati of the arguments for protection and why most economists reject them.

furtherReading.title: Protection (Encyclopaedia Britannica, 1911)
furtherReading.note: A sympathetic period account of protection as a policy and a doctrine, from Hamilton to Patten.

furtherReading.title: Report on Manufactures, by Alexander Hamilton
furtherReading.note: The 1791 report that first set out the modern case for protecting new industries.

furtherReading.title: The National System of Political Economy, by Friedrich List
furtherReading.note: List's classic argument for protection as a stage in a nation's development.

keyFigures.name: Alexander Hamilton
keyFigures.role: Wrote the Report on Manufactures (1791), the first formulation of modern protectionist doctrine

keyFigures.name: Friedrich List
keyFigures.role: German economist whose National System of Political Economy argued for infant-industry protection

keyFigures.name: Henry Charles Carey
keyFigures.role: American economist, the most influential follower of Hamilton and List

missingStatements.text: A country should build up its own manufacturing industry.
missingStatements.rationale: The founding texts make a home manufacturing industry the purpose of protection: Hamilton ties a nation's wealth, independence and security to it, and List calls a merely agricultural state a less perfect institution, dependent on the nations that buy its produce.

quotes.text: Not only the wealth, but the independence and security of a country, appear to be materially connected with the prosperity of manufactures.
quotes.where: section on the means of national supply

quotes.text: A mere agricultural State is an infinitely less perfect institution than an agricultural-manufacturing State
quotes.where: book II, chapter on nationality and the economy of the nation

quotes.text: the existence of manufacturing is necessary to the highest development of a nation

notes: Protectionism is an economic doctrine about trade and industry. Its defining sources and the texts they name (Hamilton, List, Carey, Patten) were searched for every theme: economy (wages, taxation, ownership, regulation, agriculture, infrastructure, monopolies, patents), world (immigration, colonies, peace and war, international bodies, foreign capital), government, liberty, society, culture, ecology (Patten on soil exhaustion) and technology. They take positions only on trade, industry and the world economy; they are silent on government, liberty, society, culture, religion and most ecology statements, so those are null and the audit is expected to fail the uncertainty rule honestly. The platforms of protectionist parties (the US tariff party's views on immigration, wages and education, British tariff reform) are reported in the 1911 Britannica as history and not used as tenets. Mercantilism has its own profile. Liberty Fund's Online Library of Liberty refused scripted access (403), so List was read in an archive.org copy of the Lloyd translation.
